title: Matrix products and order

source_policy: Definition-level references support the mathematical vocabulary. All stories and worked quantities are original constructed teaching scenarios, not measurements or historical events. Historical priority and notation claims require separate claim-level evidence before publication.
purpose: Follow a point through two transformations and compare the result when their order changes.
meaning: A matrix product represents successive compatible linear transformations. With column vectors, AB applies B first and then A. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, although some pairs do commute and different maps can agree on a particular input.

definition.setting: Real vector spaces with an explicit two-dimensional coordinate model.

signature.A,B: General compatible matrices in the definition; the live model restricts them to one horizontal and one vertical shear.
signature.order: B_then_A selects AB; A_then_B selects BA.
signature.intermediateX,intermediateY: Output of the first applied shear.
signature.finalX,finalY: Output of the second applied shear; finalX is the primary numeric Graph output.
signature.productA,productB,productC,productD: Selected product entries in row-major order.
signature.otherFinalX,otherFinalY,differenceX,diff: Opposite-order endpoint and signed current-minus-other endpoint differences.

conditions: Matrix multiplication requires compatible inner dimensions. In this live family both matrices are real 2 by 2 maps acting on column vectors.
AB means apply B first, then A; BA means apply A first, then B.
The live matrices are the two shears A=[[1,a],[0,1]] and B=[[1,0],[b,1]]; the control does not represent arbitrary matrices.
Each shear and either product has determinant 1, preserving signed unit area; this does not imply length or angle preservation.
Changing order need not change every input vector. Equality at one point, especially zero, does not prove AB=BA.
definition.domain_notes: In general an m by n matrix can multiply an n by p matrix, producing an m by p matrix. The live model is deliberately restricted to two real 2 by 2 shear families with bounded strengths and one bounded input point. It is not an arbitrary matrix calculator. Changing the order selects a discrete operation sequence; it does not continuously blend the matrices into a third operation. These area-preserving shears do not cover singular products or arbitrary scaling. Coordinate units are abstract unless a worked example declares compatible physical units.
definition.proof_status: Definition-level reference; worked properties are author-derived for stated assumptions. Independent mathematical review pending.

grammar.formation_rule: A=[[1,a],[0,1]], B=[[1,0],[b,1]]. B_then_A: intermediate=(x,b*x+y); final=(x+a*(b*x+y),b*x+y); product=[[1+a*b,a],[b,1]]. A_then_B: intermediate=(x+a*y,y); final=(x+a*y,b*(x+a*y)+y); product=[[1,a],[b,1+a*b]]. output=finalX; determinant=1. otherFinalX/Y are the opposite-order result; differenceX/Y=finalX/Y-otherFinalX/Y.
grammar.precedence: Scale components before adding. Matrix products act on column vectors from right to left; an ordered pair retains its stated coordinate order.

properties.claim: For this shear family, AB-BA=[[ab,0],[0,-ab]], so AB=BA exactly when ab=0.
properties.derivation: Multiply both row-column products and subtract their corresponding entries; both diagonal differences vanish precisely when ab=0.

prompts.prompt: Why does AB apply B first?
prompts.answer: In (AB)z=A(Bz), the expression Bz is evaluated before A acts on its result.

prompts.prompt: Must changing order always move the chosen point?
prompts.answer: No. Some matrices commute, and different maps can agree on a particular point such as zero.
